topIssues.title: op-node: origin prefetch ordering regression on 10-second L2 chains since v1.19.5
topIssues.author: atenalt
topIssues.body:
## Summary

We observed persistent L1-origin lag on a custom OP Stack rollup with **10-second L2 blocks** after upgrading op-node to **v1.19.9**. L2 block timestamps remain fresh and derivation stays at the configured L1 confirmation distance, but the unsafe L2 head's L1 origin falls approximately 148–149 L1 blocks behind the observed L1 head, near the Fjord 1,800-second drift limit.

Source-history analysis and controlled component tests identify an ordering change introduced by **#22241 / `4c3d0d3da6`**, first included in stable **v1.19.5**: the direct sequencer path can schedule its next build before the shared event dispatcher runs the next-origin prefetch triggered by `ForkchoiceUpdateEvent`.

This report concerns origin advancement, not a failure to produce L2 blocks. We would appreciate confirmation of whether this is an unintended regression and guidance on preserving timely origin adoption without reintroducing derivation-induced sequencer starvation.

## Environment and observations

- Observed deployed version: op-node v1.19.9; execution client op-reth v2.6.0.
- L1: Sepolia, approximately 12-second blocks.
- L2 block time: 10 seconds.
- Sequencer and verifier L1 confirmations: 15.
- Consensus-layer sync; Fjord, Granite and Holocene active; Isthmus not activated.
- CPU was not saturated during this investigation.

At a representative sample:

| Measurement | Value |
| --- | --- |
| `head_l1.number - current_l1.number` | 15 |
| `head_l1.number - unsafe_l2.l1origin.number` | 149 |
| Unsafe L2 timestamp age | approximately 3 seconds |
| Unsafe-to-safe L2 distance | approximately 20–24 blocks |

Safe/finalized progress and L1 transaction confirmations continued. Sequencing logs repeatedly showed the same origin used for two consecutive 10-second L2 blocks, for example:

```text
L2 parent  N     -> origin O
L2 parent  N+1   -> origin O
L2 parent  N+2   -> origin O+1
L2 parent  N+3   -> origin O+1
```

Reverting **only op-node** to the previously deployed v1.17.0 restored one origin advance per L2 block while behind, and the observed head-to-origin lag began decreasing (146 → 144 → 143, later 122). Execution client, batcher, RPC provider, fork schedule and confirmation settings were unchanged. This rollback was diagnostic, **not a recommendation to run an old client after Sepolia's L1 fork**; we are aware of the v1.19.5+ requirement.

## Suspected mechanism

1. The selector has cached current origin `O` and next origin `O+1`.
2. A newly inserted L2 block adopts `O+1`.
3. The direct sequencer path completes `ProcessPayload` and calls `scheduleNextAction` without requiring the shared dispatcher to finish the corresponding forkchoice-prefetch handler.
4. If the next `FindL1Origin` runs first, `CurrentAndNextOrigin` promotes cached `O+1` to current and clears the next-origin cache.
5. With no next origin cached and drift still below its limit, the selector reuses `O+1`, despite `O+2` being available and having a valid timestamp/confirmation distance.
6. The later forkchoice handler prefetches `O+2`, but the missed adoption opportunity can repeat as origins advance.

With 10-second L2 blocks, advancing an origin only once per two L2 blocks means approximately 20 seconds per origin, slower than L1's approximately 12-second block interval. Once drift approaches the limit, the synchronous-fetch fallback constrains the lag rather than restoring the intended confirmation-distance target. Faster 2-second chains can still keep up despite the missed opportunities, so the effect is more visible with a longer L2 block time.

Relevant source:

- [Sequencer concurrency change #22241](https://github.com/ethereum-optimism/optimism/pull/22241)
- [Introduction commit](https://github.com/ethereum-optimism/optimism/commit/4c3d0d3da6c9b2edd9ac93756aef5629b8a97b44)
- [v1.19.9 origin selector](https://github.com/ethereum-optimism/optimism/blob/op-node/v1.19.9/op-node/rollup/sequencing/origin_selector.go)
- [v1.19.9 sequencer](https://github.com/ethereum-optimism/optimism/blob/op-node/v1.19.9/op-node/rollup/sequencing/sequencer.go)

## Controlled source-boundary tests

We tested isolated production-source snapshots with their original module pins and checksum-verified superchain bundles, using Go 1.26.6 and test-only overlays. The probes use each snapshot's **actual Sequencer and L1OriginSelector**, existing attribute/conductor test fixtures, and a mocked successful engine insertion with deliberately controlled forkchoice-dispatch timing. Each boundary test was repeated 20 times.

The setup has current origin 818, prefetched origin 819, and origin 820 already available with a valid timestamp. The inserted child adopts 819. The question is whether the next build can run before the selector handles the child's forkchoice update.

| Source snapshot | Before prefetch fanout | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `4c3d0d3^` (`20818c5b`) | Payload success alone does not arm the next build; shared forkchoice processing precedes the next action | selects 820 |
| `4c3d0d3` | Direct insertion arms the next build independently | delayed prefetch selects 819; prefetch-first control selects 820 |
| stable v1.19.4 | same as the parent | selects 820 |
| stable v1.19.5 | same as the child | delayed prefetch selects 819; prefetch-first control selects 820 |

These are **controlled component tests, not an end-to-end historical-binary/network bisect**. They reproduce the call-site ordering change; the production v1.19.9 versus node-only rollback comparison provides separate operational evidence. Tests with Isthmus disabled and enabled both reproduced the same origin-selection outcome.

### Minimal selector-order reproducer

The following self-contained program models the triggering event order using the real selector. Run it from an upstream module checkout, for example v1.19.5, with its normal dependencies available:

```bash
go run /tmp/origin-order-repro.go
```

```go
package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "log/slog"
    "math/big"

    "github.com/ethereum-optimism/optimism/op-node/rollup"
    "github.com/ethereum-optimism/optimism/op-node/rollup/engine"
    "github.com/ethereum-optimism/optimism/op-node/rollup/sequencing"
    "github.com/ethereum-optimism/optimism/op-service/eth"
    "github.com/ethereum/go-ethereum"
    "github.com/ethereum/go-ethereum/common"
    "github.com/ethereum/go-ethereum/log"
)

type source struct {
    sequencing.L1Blocks // Unused additional methods, if present, must not be called.
    now uint64
}

func block(n uint64) eth.L1BlockRef {
    return eth.L1BlockRef{
        Number: n, Time: n * 12,
        Hash: common.BigToHash(new(big.Int).SetUint64(n)),
        ParentHash: common.BigToHash(new(big.Int).SetUint64(n - 1)),
    }
}

func (s *source) L1BlockRefByNumber(_ context.Context, n uint64) (eth.L1BlockRef, error) {
    if n + 15 > s.now / 12 {
        return eth.L1BlockRef{}, ethereum.NotFound
    }
    return block(n), nil
}

func (s *source) L1BlockRefByHash(_ context.Context, h common.Hash) (eth.L1BlockRef, error) {
    return block(h.Big().Uint64()), nil
}

func run(prefetchFirst bool, blockTime uint64) {
    ctx := context.Background()
    src := &source{now: 10000}
    cfg := &rollup.Config{BlockTime: blockTime, MaxSequencerDrift: 1800}
    logger := log.NewLogger(slog.NewTextHandler(io.Discard, nil))
    sel := sequencing.NewL1OriginSelector(ctx, logger, cfg, src)
    head := eth.L2BlockRef{Number: 100, Time: src.now, L1Origin: block(src.now/12 - 15).ID()}
    for i := 0; i < 600; i++ {
        src.now = head.Time
        ev := engine.ForkchoiceUpdateEvent{UnsafeL2Head: head}
        if prefetchFirst { sel.OnEvent(ctx, ev) }
        origin, err := sel.FindL1Origin(ctx, head)
        if err != nil { panic(err) }
        if !prefetchFirst { sel.OnEvent(ctx, ev) }
        head = eth.L2BlockRef{Number: head.Number + 1, Time: head.Time + blockTime, L1Origin: origin.ID()}
    }
    fmt.Printf("prefetchFirst=%v blockTime=%d originLag=%d drift=%d\n",
        prefetchFirst, blockTime, head.Time/12-head.L1Origin.Number,
        head.Time-block(head.L1Origin.Number).Time)
}

func main() {
    run(true, 10)
    run(false, 10)
    run(false, 2)
}
```

Observed output:

```text
prefetchFirst=true  blockTime=10 originLag=16  drift=196
prefetchFirst=false blockTime=10 originLag=149 drift=1792
prefetchFirst=false blockTime=2  originLag=15  drift=184
```

The selector-only model deliberately chooses the event order; it does not itself simulate the full driver. The separate actual-Sequencer probes above establish that the new direct-call path permits that order, while the old path required forkchoice processing before scheduling the next action.

## Downstream impact

With batcher's unchanged `max-channel-duration=100`, a large gap between current L1 head and the last submitted L1 origin causes newly opened channels to expire immediately. We observed single-L2-block channels and a higher number of small L1 submissions while origin lag exceeded that threshold. This appears to be downstream amplification, not the initiating batcher fault.

## Expected behavior / questions

- When the immediate next origin is available, confirmed and timestamp-valid, the new scheduling path should not systematically miss its adoption opportunity because the prefetch event is queued behind the next direct build.
- Can next-origin readiness be established independently of the shared dispatcher, while retaining confirmation-depth, immediate-child, timestamp and max-drift constraints and avoiding unbounded L1 RPC blocking?
- Is there an existing supported mitigation or fix for long-block-time chains that should retain post-Glamsterdam compatibility?

We searched related reports including #11960, #19263, #22821 and the receipts-prefetch changes #22861/#22863, but did not find an exact report of this long-block-time origin-progression regression. Latest stable checked on 2026-10-08 was v1.19.9. Please let us know if this should be linked to an existing issue.

topPRs.title: Glamsterdam L1 Upgrade Compatibility
topPRs.author: max-sanchez
topPRs.body:
Sepolia activates Glamsterdam ("Amsterdam" on the execution layer) on
  2026-10-06 13:53:36 UTC. This PR keeps op-node, op-batcher and op-proposer
  working when the L1 under them forks. The L2 does not activate any Amsterdam
  feature.

  Depends on hemilabs/op-geth#111, pinned here at f5c491e251ce, which adds the
  two new L1 header fields with codecs identical to upstream v1.17.7.

  ## Changes

  - **Pin op-geth f5c491e251ce** and adapt to its API (gas-limit-aware
    `ValidateOptimismExtraData` at every call site, `SetCode`/`SetBalance`
    reasons, `ChainContext` stubs, `NewBlockChain` signature).
  - **`RPCHeader` carries `blockAccessListHash` and `slotNumber`**, so op-node's
    L1 block hash verification (and the head subscription) keeps working from
    the fork block on. Without this every post-fork block fails verification and
    derivation stops.
  - **Batcher calldata gas limit** is the larger of the old and the Amsterdam
    floor (15000 + 64 gas/byte), valid on both sides of the fork. Blob
    transactions are unaffected.
  - **Beacon spec**: read `SLOT_DURATION_MS` with a fallback to
    `SECONDS_PER_SLOT` (port of upstream #23138).
  - A guard in `RPCBlock.ExecutionPayloadEnvelope` against blocks with the new
    fields, tests for the gas-limit wiring, and fixed stale test call sites.

  Receipts, deposits, the L1 attributes deposit and the proposer were traced and
  tested and need no change.

  ## Verification
  
  - Unit tests with an upstream v1.17.7 header fixture; all 53,300 Amsterdam
    headers from execution-spec-tests through every L1 header path, 0 mismatches.
  - The op-node L1 client with full verification against the live Glamsterdam
    devnet: 472 blocks across its fork boundary, 26,071 receipts, tx types 0 to 4.
  - Every batcher transaction shape accepted by upstream v1.17.7 under Amsterdam
    rules and by Hemi's op-geth under Osaka rules.
  - Six review rounds (three on this branch, three cross-cutting).
  - The heminetwork localnet (branch `max/glamsterdam-l1-migration-e2e`) now
    forks the L1 while the stack runs, with hash verification on, in blob and
    calldata mode. It passes with this branch.

topPRs.title: contracts-bedrock,op-core,op-supernode,kona: formal models and differential tests for interop message expiry
topPRs.author: karlfloersch
topPRs.body:
Adds formal models, symbolic checks and differential tests for interop message expiry and `SuperchainETHBridge` refunds (#23259). They give reviewers machine-checked evidence that the shipped design cannot pay ETH twice: a message is never both relayed on its destination and refunded on its source. These models found the pre-staged-withdrawal double spend in the earlier design, where L1 trusted the L2ToL2CrossDomainMessenger as the sender. That finding is why exports now come from the `UndeliveredMessageExporter` predeploy. They check that the landed design closes the gap. Without them, the safety argument rests on prose and unit tests.

No effect on users: everything is test or verification code. The Solidity under `test/formal/` compiles into the forge test build, and its Foundry invariant and fuzz suites run in contracts-bedrock CI with inline budgets. The Lean, Quint, Dafny, Halmos, Kontrol, hevm and EVMLean harnesses are not wired into CI; each directory's README says how to run it. The three Go/Rust tests run the real window-rule implementations against shared vectors.

The files live in a new `test/formal/expiry/` tree rather than `test/invariants/` and `test/kontrol/` because one argument spans several tools. `test/formal/expiry/README.md` maps each property to the tools that check it, and lists what is proved and what is assumed. The one-line `test-validation` exclusion is needed because these files have no matching `src/` path, as for `test/invariants/`.

Related: #23259.

Reviews: each layer was audited by a fresh-context reviewer and by two independent model reviewers; the outcomes are in each README's review log. `go-code-reviewer` and `rust-code-reviewer` are pending for the differential tests. `interop-reviewer` and `/security-review` are not run because this diff changes no production code; they apply to #23259.

topPRs.title: ci: pilot RWX with shared routing and shadow tests
topPRs.author: teddyknox
topPRs.body:
PR validation currently rebuilds op-reth in CircleCI and lacks executed RWX parity evidence. This pilot runs the complete op-reth release producer and its three associated checks alongside shared routing, Go lint/Rust formatting, Go rollup tests and four standard-contract configurations. CircleCI continues to own the required gates.

The op-reth shadow builds both release binaries, runs every selected `reth-optimism-node` test through a nextest archive, generates fresh compact vectors with pinned develop and reads them with the PR binary, and regenerates both superchain snapshots. It uses shared dependency downloads, content caching, separate native tool caches for Cargo targets and sccache, parallel codec compilers, pinned tools and SHA-bound artifacts. Checksum-matching superchain bundles retain their timestamps. Release, integration and codec consumers mount artifacts directly instead of inheriting compiler-cache layers. Every verdict and vector generation executes freshly.

Validation:

- At `0b7935e7339726c1b1166be6372fbf057fb251dd`, [native op-reth CI](https://cloud.rwx.com/optimism/runs/0d4989f8fc044b48888ba7cdda9e9b2a) passed all four workloads in **6m20s**. All 50 runnable integration cases passed; one explicitly ignored case remained in discovery. Original JUnit identities and outcomes matched [CircleCI job 5625881](https://circleci.com/gh/ethereum-optimism/optimism/5625881) exactly. All four RWX status checks are green at this head.
- Direct artifact mounts removed both compiler-cache trees from the codec verifier. Its measured preparation fell from 171s at `99ccc76a` to 2s at this head, followed by fresh execution in 5s. The final consumer received a 622 MiB binary artifact and two small vector/provenance artifacts, and its metadata confirmed the PR checkout. Both observations are single samples, with different runner-local layer states.
- Before the bundle/artifact optimizations, the complete RWX run at `d2b90241` took 13m10s initially and [5m58s with warm tool caches](https://cloud.rwx.com/optimism/runs/2c7e09f8233541869ff6fa8771b3d372). A [forced target-cache probe](https://cloud.rwx.com/optimism/runs/8545eb684d094e13abc4e91fdab645fe) after bundle retention executed snapshot preparation in 7s, with six Rust sccache hits and zero misses; fresh regeneration still ran for 24s.
- An [empty-target probe](https://cloud.rwx.com/optimism/runs/8552f40db3314cf282583313806e0be6) produced 263 Rust hits and zero misses in 36s. An [identical-input release rerun](https://cloud.rwx.com/optimism/runs/be0b0006cd5044c88739ec46cd81f2d6) reused the compiler content cache and finished the release path in 8s, including fresh binary verification. A separate warm release rebuild recorded 27 Rust hits and no misses but still spent 236s compiling/linking; content reuse and incremental reuse have different benefits.
- An [intentional CLI-only test fault](https://cloud.rwx.com/optimism/runs/add6576e7432497a8a1e3f85a40a8313) failed the task and run, preserved nextest's exit 100, and retained original JUnit and partial coverage. Committed Rust tests were unchanged.
- 22 cache/provenance/report regression tests, 35 routing scenarios, shell checks and RWX configuration validation passed. The final native artifact consumers inherited no op-reth compiler caches; only snapshot regeneration retained Cargo targets.

Implementation coverage is **10/86 expanded PR jobs, about 12%**. The [parity checklist](https://github.com/ethereum-optimism/optimism/blob/codex/rwx-ci-pilot/docs/ai/rwx-parity-todos.md) and [measurements](https://github.com/ethereum-optimism/optimism/blob/codex/rwx-ci-pilot/docs/ai/rwx-migration.md#first-hosted-measurements) track representative Rust source-change probes, repeated actual-resource timings and billed usage, smaller tool/compiler layers, and a protected cache-rebuild policy before promotion. Whole-run duration, compiler phases and billed cost remain separate measurements; declared resource classes do not prove identical hardware. Full Go/acceptance producers and consumers, remaining Rust/contracts, routing and identity cutover remain open.

Earlier Go/contract comparisons at `587b4c3a` still need authoritative CircleCI discovery, 178 contract skip reasons and fresh evidence for 17 cached Go cases. Schedules, publishing and privileged writer ownership remain with CircleCI. The cache-only RWX vault has no production credentials and restricted pilot/develop writers; remove the temporary pilot grant and evict pilot cache entries before promotion.

This single draft PR replaces #23141, #23142, #23144 and #23148 and remains the ongoing home for the pilot.

topPRs.body:
Stacked on #23102 (gen-cli); its diff shows that PR's commits until it merges.

The op-reth CLI reference is 73 pages under Node Operators › Reference, generated at v2.4.1 and three releases behind, with the same Logging and Display blocks reprinted on all 72 command pages and a 60-chain list on most of them, so a search for any common flag returns most of the tree (ethereum-optimism/solutions#1209). This replaces it with the first component on the generated, versioned reference the content guide specifies: 15 pages under `reference/op-reth/v2.4`, generated by gen-cli from the published `op-reth:v2.4.4` image in 13 seconds, with an index, one page per top-level command whose nested subcommands are headings, and a global-options page for the three sections every command repeated. The Reference tab now exists with the op-reth dropdown and its v2.4 version entry.

Effect on users: every old URL redirects. Nested subcommands land on the anchor of their heading (`db/checksum/mdbx` → `db#checksum-mdbx`), verified live with `mint dev` along with the root and overview redirects. The 69 older redirects that already pointed into the deleted tree are re-targeted so no redirect chains. The hand-written orientation page moves to Node Operators › Guides › Configuration ("Understanding the op-reth CLI"), since nothing under `reference/` is hand-written, and nine pages that linked into the old tree now link to the new one. The `op-reth node` page is 1,700 lines instead of the old tree's combined 17,700, and the chain list appears once, as a pointer to the superchain-registry. op-reth's flag catalog moves from three releases behind to current.

Effect on maintainers: `gen-op-reth-cli` is deleted; gen-cli regenerates this line with `--component op-reth --tag <tag> --image auto`, and `--check` verifies it. The nav, redirect, reference and link-policy lints pass on this branch with its own lint scripts (#23102 now carries the nav-lint change that understands `dropdowns`/`versions`, identical to #23091's, so this no longer waits on #23091). Until the tag-triggered regeneration job lands (ethereum-optimism/solutions#1518, Phase 2.2), a new op-reth release is regenerated by hand; the old tree had no working automation either (the README described one that was never registered), so this gap is not new.

Review: the deletion-reviewer agent swept the whole repository for references to the deleted URLs, nav group and generator, and verified one redirect per deleted URL, every anchored destination against the target page's headings, no chains, and no other generator or asset referencing the old tree. It found one dead link in `rust/UPDATING-RETH.md` step 9 of the reth-bump procedure (fixed), three descriptions that still said the reference was imported from the source tree or that subcommands get their own pages (fixed), and the nav-lint dependency above (resolved by carrying the change in #23102). Redirect destinations name the `v2.4` line. When a new minor line ships and becomes the default, those redirects still resolve but land on v2.4; retargeting them is a one-line job for the regeneration workflow and is tracked with the versioning work rather than done here.
